extracted.intended_audience: mathematical-olympiad students and advanced high-school/undergraduate problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter of a mathematics olympiad-style problem book (algebra and analysis) collecting theorems, solution ideas, and many contest-style problems (periodicity, Abel summation, Chebyshev/recurrence identities, matrices, mean value theorem, digit problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic functional equation (rational Möbius-type shift)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let f : R → R − {3} and suppose there exists ω > 0 such that for all x ∈ R,

f(x + ω) = ( f(x) − 5 ) / ( f(x) − 3 ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem asks to prove that f is periodic. (Use iteration/composition of the Möbius map; the displayed functional equation is the criterion to be analyzed to deduce periodicity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: D'Alembert-type functional equation implies periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : R → R satisfy f(x + y) + f(x − y) = 2 f(x) f(y) for all x, y ∈ R, and suppose there exists x0 with f(x0) = −1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: prove that f is periodic. (This is the classical cosine-type functional equation; existence of a point with value −1 provides a means to find a period via trigonometric/oscillatory solutions or to show boundedness and periodicity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation determined by value: noninjectivity ⇒ periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description:
If f : R → R is not injective and there exists g : R × R → R such that for all x, y ∈ R,

f(x + y) = g(f(x), y),
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: show that f is periodic. (Intuition: noninjectivity gives x1 ≠ x2 with f(x1)=f(x2), then comparing translations yields equality of f at shifted points, producing a nonzero period.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated quadratic map shift implies periodicity
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let f : R → R satisfy for some fixed a and for all x ∈ R,

f(x + a) = 1/2 + f(x) − f(x)^2 (as printed: f(x + a) = 1/2 + f(x) − f(x)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem parts: (a) prove that f is periodic; (b) for a = 1 give an example. (Use properties of the logistic/iterated quadratic map; the functional equation defines an iterated map conjugate to a finite orbit or a 2-periodic behavior.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness of recursively defined sequences (problem statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence {a_n} is given with 0 < a0 < a0 + a1 < 1 and (garbled printed recurrence) ... (text shows fragments 'an+1 + an − 1 an−1 for n ≥ 1 ... = 0').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: prove existence of a real number b with |a_n| ≤ b for all n. (Original page contains a concrete recurrence; use appropriate inequalities/Abel summation or induction. The statement in the source is partially corrupted here.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear second-order recurrence periodicity condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Find all α ∈ R with the property that any sequence satisfying x_{n+1} + x_{n−1} = α x_n (n ∈ N) is periodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: determine parameter α for which all solutions of the linear recurrence are periodic. (Use characteristic equation r^2 − α r + 1 = 0 and analyze roots on the unit circle / rational multiples of π leading to periodic sequences.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Period irrationality from infinite integer sampling values
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : R → R is periodic and the set { f(n) | n ∈ N } has infinitely many elements, then the period of f is irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim: rational periods induce a finite orbit on integer arguments (mod period) so an infinite image set forces irrational period. (Use contradiction: a rational period p = r/s gives periodicity modulo integers leading to repetition of f(n) values.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonperiodicity of sin(f(x)) for divergent f and derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f : R → R be differentiable with continuous derivative such that lim_{x→∞} f(x) = lim_{x→∞} f'(x) = ∞. Then g(x) = sin(f(x)) is not periodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idea: if f and f' both diverge to infinity, f(x) grows without bound and its increments and local behaviour preclude the regular repeating structure needed for sin(f(x)) to be periodic; use monotonicity or growth to derive contradiction with periodicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity of last-digit sequences of power-sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Let b_n be the last digit of 1^1 + 2^2 + 3^3 + ··· + n^n. Then the sequence {b_n} is periodic with period 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modular arithmetic and Euler/Fermat-type periodicity of k^k modulo 10 and consider modulo 2 and 5 (CRT) to obtain period 100.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity-based integer sequence eventually periodic
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let a be an odd positive integer and b a positive integer. Define u_0 = b and for n ∈ N,

u_{n+1} = { 1/2 * u_n, if u_n is even; (u_n + a)/2, otherwise }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) Show u_n ≤ a for some n. (b) Show the sequence {u_n} is eventually periodic. (Use descent on value and pigeonhole/finiteness of residues modulo a or parity cycles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Eventual periodicity from divisibility condition in integer sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive integers a_1, a_2, a_3, ... each ≤ 1988 satisfy: for all positive m, n, a_m + a_n is divisible by a_{m+n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem: Prove the sequence is periodic from some point onwards. (Use boundedness and divisibility constraints to show values must repeat, hence eventual periodicity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear integral equalities imply linearity of monotone function
rubrics_metrics.description:
Let f : R → R be monotonic and suppose there exist real a, b, c, d with a ≠ 0, c ≠ 0 such that for all x,

∫_{x}^{x+√3} f(t) dt = a x + b,

and

∫_{x}^{x+√2} f(t) dt = c x + d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion: prove f is linear, f(x) = m x + n. (Differentiate the equalities with respect to x, use monotonicity and the two distinct interval lengths to solve for f.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abel summation formula (discrete integration by parts)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the discrete analogue of integration by parts. Use by choosing sequences s_i = partial sums of a's and t_i derived from b's to transform sums; widely useful for rearrangement inequalities, bounding sums, and proving combinatorial/number-theoretic identities. Examples on the page include polygonal line application and Kedlaya IMO-type problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygonal-line nonclosure lemma via Abel summation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a polygonal line P_0 P_1 ... P_n with all consecutive angles equal (measured clockwise) and strictly decreasing side lengths P_0P_1 > P_1P_2 > ... > P_{n−1}P_n, then P_0 and P_n cannot coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses complex coordinates and Abel summation to express P_n coordinate as a telescoped sum, then uses triangle inequality and |z|=1 to rule out zero. (Shows application pattern of Abel summation to complex sums.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Kedlaya-type equality-of-sequences criterion (pair-difference multiset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a_1 ≤ ... ≤ a_n and b_1 ≤ ... ≤ b_n be nondecreasing with partial-sum inequalities a_1+...+a_i ≤ b_1+...+b_i for i=1,...,n−1 and equality of total sums; suppose for every real m the number of pairs (i,j) with a_i − a_j = m equals the number of pairs (k,l) with b_k − b_l = m. Then a_i = b_i for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two solutions are given using Abel summation applied to appropriate sequences and/or leveraging equality of sums of pairwise differences and of squared differences to deduce termwise equality. Pattern: equidistribution of pairwise differences + majorization ⇒ equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation xn + x^{-n} as integer polynomial in x + x^{-1} (Chebyshev-type polynomials)
rubrics_metrics.description: For x ≠ 0, the quantity x^n + x^{-n} can be written as a polynomial P_n(x + x^{-1}) with integer coefficients; P_0(X)=2, P_1(X)=X, P_2(X)=X^2−2, P_3(X)=X^3−3X, and recurrence relations follow from de Moivre/type identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurrence xn+1 + x^{-(n+1)} = (x + x^{-1})(xn + x^{-n}) − (xn−1 + x^{-(n−1)}). Applications include irrationality proofs (e.g., cos 1° irrational) and solving functional equations involving x + 1/x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix determinant identity det(I − AB) = det(I − BA) and invertibility corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: For n × n matrices A, B over reals (or any commutative field), det(I_n − AB) = det(I_n − BA). Consequently, if I_n − AB is invertible then so is I_n − BA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: handle invertible B first via similarity B^{-1}(I − BA)B = I − AB; extend to noninvertible B using polynomial identity in parameter x and continuity/polynomial identity lemma. A direct constructive inverse is also provided: if V = (I − AB)^{-1} then (I + B V A)(I − BA) = I, so I + B V A is inverse of I − BA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolle's and Mean Value Theorem (Lagrange) and Cauchy generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolle: If f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b) then ∃ c ∈ (a,b) with f'(c)=0. Lagrange (Mean Value Theorem): If f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b) then ∃ c with (f(b)−f(a))/(b−a)=f'(c). Cauchy: For f,g continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), ∃ c with (f(b)−f(a)) g'(c) = (g(b)−g(a)) f'(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are basic calculus tools; use by applying Rolle to constructed auxiliary functions (e.g., H(x) as combination) to get desired equalities. Many contest problems use these to deduce impossibility or existence of real roots, bounds on derivatives, or algebraic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application example: using Mean Value Theorem to rule out extraneous exponent equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Example problem: Show that apart from x=0 and x=1, there are no real x satisfying 2^x + 5^x = 3^x + 4^x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat x as fixed exponent function f(t)=t^x and apply the mean value theorem on disjoint intervals [2,3] and [4,5] to derive contradiction from distinct mean-value points and resulting equality constraints. This demonstrates the pattern of evaluating power functions and comparing derivatives via MVT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sierpiński decomposition: any real function as sum of two intermediate-value-property functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every function f : R → R can be written as f = g + h where g and h each have the intermediate value property (Darboux functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof uses decimal expansions of x and splits digits into two subsequences (odd and even positions) to define g and h based on long-tail digit patterns so that on any interval the restrictions of g and h are surjective, hence have the intermediate value property. This is a construction pattern to produce Darboux functions summing to an arbitrary f.
